name: Mars Polar Lander
mission: Mars Polar Lander / Deep Space 2 (Mars Surveyor '98)

location.name: South polar layered terrain (targeted site; never found)

headline: A polar lander that fell silent on the way down and has never been found
story: On 3 December 1999, Mars Polar Lander sent its last signal to Earth just before it plunged into the Martian atmosphere. It was aiming for the layered terrain near the edge of the south polar cap, carrying a robotic arm to dig for water ice and two Deep Space 2 microprobes. By design, it sent no data during the descent. The call expected after landing never came.

Engineers kept listening for weeks. Mars Global Surveyor began photographing the landing zone on 16 December, and on 17 January 2000 NASA stopped trying to reach the lander. A review board found the probable cause: as the legs unfolded, they could send a false touchdown signal. At 40 meters up, the engines would have shut off, leaving the lander to hit the ground at about 22 meters per second.

In 2005, a camera team thought it had spotted the lander's parachute in old images. A sharper picture showed only a small hill. Mars Polar Lander has never been found. Whatever is left of it lies somewhere in a landing zone about 200 kilometers long near 76 degrees south, unseen for more than a quarter of a century.

facts.label: Launched
facts.value: 3 January 1999, Cape Canaveral, on a Delta II

facts.label: Last contact
facts.value: 3 December 1999, about 20:00 UTC, just before atmospheric entry

facts.label: Probable cause
facts.value: A false touchdown signal shut off the engines about 40 m above the surface

facts.label: Targeted site
facts.value: About 76° S, 195° W (165° E), near the south polar cap

images.caption: November 1998, Kennedy Space Center: the two Deep Space 2 microprobes mounted on opposite sides of Mars Polar Lander, weeks before launch.
3 January 1999: a Delta II rocket lifts off from Cape Canaveral with Mars Polar Lander, beginning an 11-month journey to Mars.
The search begins: Mars Global Surveyor's first image of the landing zone, taken 16 December 1999. At 1.5 meters per pixel, the lander would be only a few pixels across.
